10034714:
February 27, 2025
LD 366 "An Act to Ensure Consistency of Income Tax Deductions for Retired Members of the
Uniformed Services"
Chairwoman Grohoski, Chairwoman Cloutier, and Honorable Members of the Taxation Committee. My name is Alan Echt, I volunteer for the Commissioned Officers Association of the U.S. Public Health Service, and I am a past member of their Boad of Directors. I am a retired USPHS officer, my wife was born and raised in Portland, and we sent our oldest kid to Colby College. My wife and I live in Ohio, and we sometimes talk about returning to Maine when she retires. Ohio fully exempts my USPHS retirement pay from state income tax.
I am testifying in support of LD 366, "An Act to Ensure Consistency of Income Tax Deductions for Retired Members of the Uniformed Services." Maine currently tax-exempts the military pensions of retired members of the Army, Navy, Marine Corps, Coast Guard and Air Force, neglecting those retirees who served in the other three U.S. uniformed services. This bill represents an opportunity to not only correct that disparity for Maine veterans who served in the Space Force, NOAA Commissioned Officer Corps, and Public Health Service Commissioned Corps, but it is also an opportunity to attract retired professionals to Maine. NOAA Corps officers are highly trained engineers and scientists. Currently, one active-duty NOAA Corps officer serves in Maine and four retirees live here. Public Health Service veterans are all degreed professionals - nurses, physicians, pharmacists, scientists, veterinarians, engineers, and members of other professions. There are currently seven active-duty USPHS officers serving in Maine and 32 USPHS retirees call Maine home.
Those NOAA Corps and USPHS retirees typically have other income sources that Maine can tax, resulting in additional revenue. Also, they will not increase the burden on other state programs such as Medicaid, since they are all eligible for TRICARE coverage and many also qualify for VA healthcare. Among Maine's neighbors, Massachusetts fully tax-exempts the retirement pay of all eight uniformed services and Vermont offers a partial income tax deduction. New Hampshire doesn't tax earned income.
LD 366 represents a simple policy amendment for the Taxation Committee that will ensure fairness for all Maine Veterans. Thank you for your thoughtful consideration of this important policy initiative, and for all you do for the State of Maine.
CAPT (Ret) Alan Echt, USPHS, MPH, DrPH, CIH

of the Uniformed Services" Joint Standing Committee on Taxation
Thursday February 27, 2025

Chairwoman Grohoski, Chairwoman Cloutier, and Honorable Members of the Taxation
Committee:
My name is Brad Farrin and I serve Senate District 3. I am here today to present LD 366, "An
Act to Ensure Consistency ofIncome Tax Deductions for Retired Members of the Uniformed
Services."
This past fall I was made aware made of a limitation under Maine's current tax exemption statute for retired military pay. Currently the statute exempts retired military pay for five of the eight federally-recognized uniformed services: Army, Navy, Air Force, Marine Corps and Coast
Guard. It excludes Space Force, National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, (NOAA)
and United States Public Health Service (USPHS) which, in turn, would be a deterrent for these retired military members to select Maine as a place to retire. Currently, 38 states fully exempt all Uniformed Services military retired pay from state tax; Maryland is introducing legislation this
year. There are approximately 33 retirees from NOAA and the USPHS currently living in
Maine.
I urge the Committee to support LD 366. This is a bill that will not only bring fairness to our retirees `who have served in Space Force, NOAA, and Public Health Service but create an
opportunity to attract professional retirees to Maine. These retirees are generally in their prime working years (3 Os-50s) and have other income that Maine will be able to tax resulting in increased revenue for the state.
LD 366 represents a simple policy amendment for the Taxation Committee that will ensure
fairness for our Uniformed Services Retirees and make Maine a more desirable home for this group of retirees. Thank you for your consideration of this important policy initiative.

10033919:
February 27, 2025
LD 366 "An Act to Ensure Consistency of Income Tax Deductions for Retired Members of the
Uniformed Services"
Chairwoman Grohoski, Chairwoman Cloutier, and Honorable Members of the Taxation Committee- my name is Brenda Pennels. I am a Scarbrough resident and serve as Maine's Civilian Aide to the Secretary of the Army (CASA), the President of the Maine Chapter of the Military Officers Association of America, and Aide de Camp for Governor Mills. I am a veteran Army Officer with 20 years of service and work for Martin's Point Health Care in Portland as the Strategic Relations Manager for the Uniformed Services Family Health Plan. I am testifying in support of LD 366, "An Act to Ensure Consistency of Income Tax Deductions for Retired Members of the Uniformed Services." Martin's Point Healthcare has been serving Military families in Maine for 44years. With our headquarters' located in Portland, the Marine Hospital which is situated in the center of our campus is a historic relic that dates back to 1858. The Marine Hospital was established to care for ill or injured merchant seamen and coastal lighthouse keepers and their families. The facility also served as a Union hospital during the Civil War and eventually came under the administration of the US Public Health Service (PHS). As a DOD contractor and TRICARE Provider, Martin's Point enrolls eligible retirees from all 8 branches of the Uniformed Services, including the Space Force, NOAA and US Public Health Service.
The exclusion of the tax exemption in our statute for retirees from US Public Health Service, NOAA and the Space Force was first brought to my attention a year ago by an actively serving USPHS Captain (formerly a Naval Officer) currently assigned to the Boston Coast Guard Station as a Regional Behavioral Health Provider. This officer has deep connections to Maine, spending summers in Kennebunkport, attending the University of New England in Biddeford for graduate school , and ultimately purchasing his own home in Kennebunkport in 2020 in anticipation of his retirement from the USPHS. Upon retirement he plans to move to move his family to Maine and continue to work supporting the behavioral health needs of currently serving servicemembers and veterans.
LD366 represents an opportunity to not only bring fairness to our retirees who have served in the Space Force, NOAA, and the US Public Health Service, but it is also an opportunity to attract professional retirees to Maine that possess the training, skills and education that will benefit our state. Many of these retirees, like the Captain I have mentioned in this testimony, are still of working age and will have other taxable income resulting in increased state revenue. Additionally, as these retirees are all TRICARE eligible, which is a Federal entitlement, they will not increase the burden on state programs such as Medicaid.

LD 366 is a modest policy amendment that will not only provide significant benefits to our state, it will ensure fairness and consistency for our Uniformed Services Retirees. Thank you for your thoughtful consideration of this important policy initiative, and for all you do for the State of Maine.
Brenda Pennels Civilian Aide to the Secretary of the Army, Maine

Chairwoman Grohoski, Chairwoman Cloutier, and Honorable Members of the Taxation

My name is Joan Hunter. I'm a retired Rear Admiral in the U.S. Public Health Service
Commissioned Corps with 29 years of service. I am currently on the Board of Directors for the National Alliance on Mental Illness for Maine, a Board Member for the Military Officers
Association of America (MOAA-national), and a member of the MOAA Southern Maine
Chapter.
I am here today to strongly urge your support for LD 366. This important proposed legislation
will ensure consistency of state tax deductions for all our Nation's eight Uniformed Services.
The USPHS was established in 1798 as a cadre of officers dedicated to serving sick and injured
seamen as part of the Marine Hospital Service. Today we are a cadre of approximately 6000 trained, health professionals within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. Our
mission is: "...to protect, promote and advance the health and safety of our Nation."
Our physicians, nurses, pharmacists, dentists, veterinarians, scientists, engineers, and other health professionals conduct medical and behavioral health research, protect our citizens against unsafe medical products, and respond to the health care needs of populations during national
emergencies, pandemics, and natural disasters. For example, during the Global War on Terror,
my orders were to design, build and direct the first psychological health program for our -
National Guard soldiers and airmen in all 54 states and territories.
USPHS ofiicers have the same ethical standards and professional conduct requirements as our "sister services". We are required to successfully train and maintain proficiency and readiness for deployment. We take the same oath of ofiice as our Armed Service Members, earn the same military rank and pay grades, eam the same retirement pay and benefits, are covered by the GI Bill, are eligible for TRICARE military health care system, receive a formal discharge (DD2l4)
and earn benefits for care by the Veterans Administration.
It is without hesitation I support and thank you for your effort to recognize the need for
consistency among all eight of our Nation's Uniformed Services.
Respectfully,
Joan Hunter, RN, MSW
RADM, USPHS (Retired)
10034220:
TESTIMONY OF MICHAEL J. ALLEN, ASSOCIATE COMMISSIONER FOR TAX POLICY
DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE AND FINANCIAL SERVICES
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Taxation Hearing Date: February 27, 2025
LD 366 - "An Act to Ensure Consistency of Income Tax Deductions for Retired Members of the Uniformed Services"
Senator Grohoski, Representative Cloutier, and members of the Taxation Committee - good afternoon, my name is Michael Allen, Associate Commissioner for Tax Policy in the Department of Administrative and Financial Services. I am testifying at the request of the Administration Neither For Nor Against LD 366, "An Act to Ensure Consistency of Income Tax Deductions for Retired Members of the Uniformed Services."
This bill expands the Maine pension income deduction by extending the definition of "military retirement plan" to include benefits received as a result of service in the active or reserve components of the United States Department of Commerce, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, and the United States Public Health Service.
It is not clear whether the bill intends to limit the deduction to the uniformed services of the United States Department of Commerce, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, and the United States Public Health Service or if the deduction is to apply more broadly. In either case, the intended recipients of the deduction should be clarified.
Currently, military retirement pay is fully exempt from Maine individual income tax. Military retirement plans include benefits received as a result of
1

service in the active or reserve components of the United States Army, Navy, Air Force, Marines, Coast Guard, or Space Force. The pension income deduction for non-military pension income is limited to the maximum annual benefit that an individual may receive at retirement age under the federal Social Security Act reduced by the amount of social security benefits received by the taxpayer.
The Administration notes the following technical issues: � The bill does not contain an application date. � The bill should clarify whether the increased pension income deduction applies only to retirees of the applicable United States Commissioned Corps of Uniformed Services, or if the increased pension income deduction applies to all retirees receiving pension benefits as a result of service performed at any of these federal agencies. � Section 1 of the bill is unnecessary because 36 M.R.S. � 5122(2)(M) only applies to tax years beginning before January 1, 2014.
The preliminary estimated fiscal impact is a revenue loss of less than $100,000 per year.
The preliminary estimated administrative costs are nominal and can be absorbed within current budgetary allotments.
The Administration looks forward to working with the Committee on the bill; representatives from MRS will be here for the Work Session to provide additional information and respond in detail to the Committee's questions.
